{{Short description|Concept in quantum mechanics}}
{{about||the quantum master equation in quantum field theory|Batalin–Vilkovisky formalism}}
[[File:Master equation unravelings.svg|thumb|265x265px|The evolution of the z-component of the Bloch vector of a two-level atom undergoing damped Rabi oscillations as predicted by its master equation (bottom), compared to two measurement choices (photon-counting measurements and homodyne detection).]]
In [[quantum information]], a '''quantum master equation''' is a general equation describing the evolution of a quantum system interacting with its environment. They are a generalization of [[master equation|master equations]], equations that describe the evolution of probabilistic combination of states.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Campaioli |first=Francesco |last2=Cole |first2=Jared H. |last3=Hapuarachchi |first3=Harini |date=2024-06-10 |title=Quantum Master Equations: Tips and Tricks for Quantum Optics, Quantum Computing, and Beyond |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.020202 |journal=PRX Quantum |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.020202 |issn=2691-3399|doi-access=free }}</ref> Quantum master equations are differential equations for a system's [[density matrix]], a matrix descriptions of the quantum system.

Rather than just a system of differential equations for a set of probabilities (which only constitutes the diagonal elements of a [[density matrix]]), quantum master equations are differential equations for the entire density matrix, including [[off-diagonal element]]s. A density matrix with only diagonal elements can be modeled as a classical random process, therefore such an "ordinary" master equation is considered classical. Off-diagonal elements represent [[quantum coherence]] which is a physical characteristic that is intrinsically quantum mechanical.

Some quantum master equations, such as the [[Nakajima–Zwanzig equation]], are formally exact, but are in general as difficult to solve as the full quantum problem. Instead, many master equations take the [[Markov property|Markovian]] approximation to achieve reduced dynamics. This approximation assumes that the environment, or bath, is memoryless. Approximate [[Markov property|Markovian]] quantum master equations include the [[Redfield equation]] and [[Lindblad equation]]. These equations are very easy to solve, but are not generally accurate for all systems.

Some modern approximations based on quantum master equations, which show better agreement with exact numerical calculations in some cases, include the polaron transformed quantum master equation and the VPQME (variational polaron transformed quantum master equation).<ref name=McCutcheon>{{cite journal|author=D. McCutcheon, N. S. Dattani, E. Gauger, B. Lovett, A. Nazir|title=A general approach to quantum dynamics using a variational master equation: Application to phonon-damped Rabi rotations in quantum dots|journal=Physical Review B|date=25 August 2011|volume=84|issue=8|page=081305R|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.84.081305|arxiv=1105.6015|bibcode=2011PhRvB..84h1305M|s2cid=119275166}}</ref>

Numerically exact approaches to the kinds of problems to which master equations are usually applied include numerical [[Feynman integral]]s,<ref name=Dattani4>{{Citation | last = Dattani | first = Nike | year = 2013   |title=FeynDyn: A MATLAB program for fast numerical Feynman integral calculations for open quantum system dynamics on GPUs | journal = Computer Physics Communications | volume = 184 | issue = 12 | pages = 2828–2833 | bibcode = 2013CoPhC.184.2828D | doi = 10.1016/j.cpc.2013.07.001 | arxiv = 1205.6872 | s2cid = 41378038 }}</ref> [[quantum Monte Carlo]], [[Density matrix renormalization group|DMRG]]<ref name="Prior_DMRG">{{cite journal |last1=Prior |first1=Javier |title=Efficient Simulation of Strong System-Environment Interactions |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |date=30 July 2010 |volume=105 |issue=5 |article-number=050404 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.050404 |pmid=20867899 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.050404 |access-date=2 June 2021|arxiv=1003.5503 |bibcode=2010PhRvL.105e0404P |s2cid=27896369 }}</ref> and [[Numerical renormalization group|NRG]], [[Multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree|MCTDH]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Haobin |title=A multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree simulation of the reaction-coordinate spin-boson model employing an interaction picture |journal=J. Chem. Phys. |date=24 March 2017 |volume=146 |issue=12 |page=124112 |doi=10.1063/1.4978901 |pmid=28388113 |bibcode=2017JChPh.146l4112W |osti=1497842 |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.4978901 |access-date=2 June 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[hierarchical equations of motion|HEOM]].

== Background and motivation ==
The time evolution of a closed quantum system is described by the [[Schrödinger equation]],

<math display="block">i\dot{\psi} = H\psi 
\qquad
\psi_t = U_t \psi_0 ,</math>

For more than one parameter, such as in an entangled state or a classical ensemble of quantum states, the density matrix is instead used. For the density matrix, the time evolution is given by the [[von Neumann equation]],

<math display="block">\dot{\rho} = -i[H,\rho]
\qquad
\rho_t = U_t \rho_0 U_t^{\dagger} </math>

However, this still describes a closed system. Instead, the system is described by the evolution law

<math display="block">\rho' = \Lambda \rho 
= \sum_{\alpha} K_{\alpha} \rho K_{\alpha}^{\dagger} , \quad\textrm{where}\quad \sum_{\alpha} K_{\alpha}K_{\alpha}^{\dagger} = I
 </math>

This is not yet a quantum master equation since it is not a differential equation. In the Markovian approximation, this law gives:

<math display="block">\frac{d\rho}{dt} = \mathcal{L}\rho 
\qquad 
\rho_t = e^{t\mathcal{L}}\,\rho_0 ,
 </math>

which is a master equation for <math>\rho
 </math> in the Markovian approximation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chruściński |first=Dariusz |last2=Pascazio |first2=Saverio |date=2017 |title=A Brief History of the GKLS Equation |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S1230161217400017 |journal=Open Systems & Information Dynamics |volume=24 |issue=03 |pages=1740001 |doi=10.1142/S1230161217400017 |issn=1230-1612|arxiv=1710.05993 }}</ref>
